# 1. Architecture Overview

A **compute node** (the protocol calls it a *calculation member*) is an external gRPC client that runs your code inside entity workflows. The platform delegates work to it over a persistent bidirectional gRPC stream, and the compute node returns results on the same stream. For the rationale behind preferring gRPC over HTTP for compute nodes, see [APIs and surfaces](/concepts/apis-and-surfaces/).

```
┌──────────────────────┐         gRPC (bidirectional stream)         ┌─────────────────────────┐
│   Cyoda Platform     │ ◄──────────────────────────────────────────►│  Your Compute Node      │
│                      │    CloudEvent (Protobuf, JSON payload)      │  (Calculation Member)   │
│  ┌────────────────┐  │                                             │                         │
│  │ Workflow Engine│  │  1. Client opens stream, sends Join         │  ┌───────────────────┐  │
│  │                │  │  2. Server responds with Greet              │  │ Business Logic    │  │
│  │  - Processors  │──┼──3. Server pushes callout requests──────────┼──│                   │  │
│  │  - Criteria    │  │     (processor, criteria, function)         │  │ - Data transforms │  │
│  │  - Schedules   │  │  4. Client returns responses                │  │ - Criteria checks │  │
│  │                │  │  5. Server probes liveness; client acks     │  │ - Fire times      │  │
│  └────────────────┘  │                                             │  └───────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────┘                                             └─────────────────────────┘
```

Each piece of work sent to a compute node is a **callout**. There are three kinds:

| Use Case | Description | Request Type | Response Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Processing** | Perform actions during a workflow transition: compute new entity data, read or write *other* entities, call other systems. | `EntityProcessorCalculationRequest` | `EntityProcessorCalculationResponse` |
| **Criteria Evaluation** | Evaluate a boolean condition (for example, "should this transition fire?"). | `EntityCriteriaCalculationRequest` | `EntityCriteriaCalculationResponse` |
| **Function** | Compute and return a declared typed value without side effects. Currently the firing time of a [scheduled transition](/build/scheduled-transitions/). | `EntityFunctionCalculationRequest` | `EntityFunctionCalculationResponse` |

A compute node may also call back into the platform while it handles a callout, over HTTP or gRPC. Those requests are **callbacks**; see [Section 10.3.1](#1031-transaction-joined-callbacks).

## 1.1 Protocol Summary

- **Transport**: gRPC bidirectional streaming via `CloudEventsService.startStreaming`, on the gRPC port (default `9090`).
- **Message format**: [CNCF CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io/) Protobuf envelope with a JSON `text_data` payload.
- **Authentication**: the compute node's own `client_credentials` token as `authorization: Bearer <token>` gRPC metadata. See [Section 2.2](#22-authentication-token).
- **Identity on callouts**: every callout carries the principal the work is *attributed* to and the principal that *executes* it, as CloudEvent attributes. See [Section 9](#9-auth-context-on-incoming-requests).
- **Platform time on callouts**: every callout carries the platform clock's time in the standard CloudEvent `time` attribute.
- **Serialization**: all payloads are JSON inside CloudEvent `text_data`, not binary protobuf.

# 2. Prerequisites

## 2.1 Proto Definitions

Your client needs two proto files to generate gRPC stubs:

- **`cloudevents.proto`**: the standard CloudEvents Protobuf message definition (package `io.cloudevents.v1`).
- **`cyoda-cloud-api.proto`**: the Cyoda service definition (package `org.cyoda.cloud.api.grpc`).

`cyoda help grpc proto` prints both, separated by comments. Save them as `proto/cyoda/cyoda-cloud-api.proto` and `proto/cloudevents/cloudevents.proto`. The server does not serve gRPC reflection, so tools such as `grpcurl` need the files on disk.

The service definition for the compute-node stream:

```protobuf
service CloudEventsService {
  rpc startStreaming(stream io.cloudevents.v1.CloudEvent) returns (stream io.cloudevents.v1.CloudEvent);
  // entityManage, entityManageCollection, entityModelManage,
  // entitySearch and entitySearchCollection are also served (see cyoda help grpc)
}
```

The CloudEvent message:

```protobuf
message CloudEvent {
  string id = 1;          // Unique event ID (UUID recommended)
  string source = 2;      // URI-reference identifying the event source
  string spec_version = 3; // Must be "1.0"
  string type = 4;        // Event type string (see Section 4)

  map<string, CloudEventAttributeValue> attributes = 5;

  oneof data {
    bytes binary_data = 6;
    string text_data = 7;       // ← Used by Cyoda (JSON payload)
    google.protobuf.Any proto_data = 8;
  }
}
```

Go compute nodes can import the generated types instead of generating their own: `github.com/cyoda/cyoda-go/api/grpc/cyoda` (the service) and `github.com/cyoda/cyoda-go/api/grpc/cloudevents` (the envelope).

## 2.2 Authentication Token

A compute node opens its stream with **its own client's token**: an access token from the `client_credentials` grant, issued to an M2M client of your tenant by `POST /api/tenants/{tenant}/oauth/token`. The token is a service principal holding `ROLE_M2M`. How to create the client and fetch its token is set out in [Authenticating applications](/build/authenticating-applications/).

Give each compute-node service a plain client of its own, shared by all its replicas, so that it can be rotated or revoked alone and so that the executor recorded on every change names the compute node.

Every other kind of token is refused with gRPC `PermissionDenied`:

- an on-behalf-of token from the token exchange (it states a user, not a compute node);
- a token from `cyoda token` (the platform operator's);
- any token without `ROLE_M2M`.

**The stream outlives its token.** The token is checked when the stream opens. Its expiry does not end the stream, and the compute node does not reconnect when it fetches a new token. Instead, the server reads the stream's client from its store when the stream opens and every 60 seconds after. When the client has been deleted, or its secret has been reset since the token was issued, the stream is refused, or closed within a minute, with `Unauthenticated`.

**Callbacks use a current token.** Each callback the compute node makes carries its client's current `client_credentials` token. Cache the token and fetch a new one when less than 60 seconds of its life remain.

**Mock IAM mode.** With `CYODA_IAM_MODE=mock`, no token is needed. The mock principal opens a stream when `CYODA_IAM_MOCK_KIND` is `service` (the default) and `CYODA_IAM_MOCK_ROLES` holds `ROLE_M2M` (the default does). With `CYODA_IAM_MOCK_KIND=user` or `system` the stream is refused with `PermissionDenied`.

## 2.3 Dependencies (Java/Kotlin Example)

For JVM-based clients, the recommended dependencies are:

- `io.grpc:grpc-stub`, `io.grpc:grpc-protobuf`, `io.grpc:grpc-netty-shaded`: gRPC runtime
- `io.cloudevents:cloudevents-protobuf`: CloudEvents SDK Protobuf format support
- `io.cloudevents:cloudevents-core`: CloudEvents SDK core
- `com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind`: JSON serialization

# 3. Connection Setup

The gRPC listener has three properties to plan for:

- **Port.** `CYODA_GRPC_PORT`, default `9090`.
- **Bind address.** `CYODA_GRPC_BIND_ADDRESS` defaults to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), so only a compute node on the same host can connect. Set it to `0.0.0.0` (or `::`) when compute nodes run on other hosts, or when cyoda runs in a container whose port is mapped.
- **Plaintext.** The listener has no TLS of its own. In production, TLS is terminated by the ingress, gateway or service mesh in front of it (the Helm chart's `ingress.grpc.tls`), and the compute node connects through it and verifies the server certificate. Plaintext is for localhost or a private Docker network during development.

## 3.1 Create the gRPC Channel

```java
// Production: through the TLS-terminating ingress
ManagedChannel channel = ManagedChannelBuilder
    .forAddress("cyoda-grpc.example.com", 443)
    .useTransportSecurity()
    .keepAliveTime(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .keepAliveTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build();
```

For local development against a cyoda process on the same host:

```java
ManagedChannel channel = ManagedChannelBuilder
    .forAddress("localhost", 9090)
    .usePlaintext()
    .build();
```

The server accepts transport-level pings from a client as often as every 5 seconds, so a normal `keepAliveTime` is never penalised.

## 3.2 Attach Credentials

Create a `CallCredentials` implementation that injects the `authorization` metadata:

```java
CallCredentials callCredentials = new CallCredentials() {
    @Override
    public void applyRequestMetadata(RequestInfo requestInfo, Executor executor, MetadataApplier applier) {
        executor.execute(() -> {
            Metadata headers = new Metadata();
            headers.put(
                Metadata.Key.of("Authorization", Metadata.ASCII_STRING_MARSHALLER),
                "Bearer " + clientTokenSupplier.get()  // current client_credentials token
            );
            applier.apply(headers);
        });
    }
};
```

`clientTokenSupplier` returns the compute node's cached `client_credentials` token and fetches a new one when it is close to expiry.

## 3.3 Create the Stub

```java
CloudEventsServiceGrpc.CloudEventsServiceStub asyncStub = CloudEventsServiceGrpc
    .newStub(channel)
    .withCallCredentials(callCredentials)
    .withWaitForReady();   // Wait for the channel to become ready before sending
```

---

# 4. CloudEvent Type System

Every message on the stream is a CloudEvent with a `type` field that determines how to deserialize the JSON `text_data`. Your client must handle the following types:

| CloudEvent `type` | Direction | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `CalculationMemberJoinEvent` | Client → Server | Register as a compute member. Must be the first message. |
| `CalculationMemberGreetEvent` | Server → Client | Server confirms registration. Always the first event the server sends. |
| `CalculationMemberKeepAliveEvent` | Server → Client; optionally Client → Server | Liveness probe. Neither side replies to a keep-alive it receives, apart from the client's ack below. |
| `EventAckResponse` | Client → Server | Acknowledges a server event (a keep-alive probe or the greet) that needs no other answer. |
| `EntityProcessorCalculationRequest` | Server → Client | Process entity data |
| `EntityProcessorCalculationResponse` | Client → Server | Return processed entity data |
| `EntityCriteriaCalculationRequest` | Server → Client | Evaluate a boolean criterion |
| `EntityCriteriaCalculationResponse` | Client → Server | Return criterion result |
| `EntityFunctionCalculationRequest` | Server → Client | Compute a typed value (no side effects) |
| `EntityFunctionCalculationResponse` | Client → Server | Return the typed result |

## 4.1 Building a CloudEvent

To send a CloudEvent on the stream (Java/Kotlin with CloudEvents SDK):

```java
// 1. Build the CloudEvents SDK event
io.cloudevents.CloudEvent sdkEvent = CloudEventBuilder.v1()
    .withType("CalculationMemberJoinEvent")   // Must match the type table above
    .withSource(URI.create("my-compute-node"))
    .withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
    .withData(PojoCloudEventData.wrap(event, e -> objectMapper.writeValueAsBytes(e)))
    .build();

// 2. Serialize to Protobuf
EventFormat protobufFormat = EventFormatProvider.getInstance()
    .resolveFormat("application/cloudevents+protobuf");
byte[] protoBytes = protobufFormat.serialize(sdkEvent);

// 3. Parse to the gRPC CloudEvent message
io.cloudevents.v1.proto.CloudEvent grpcEvent =
    io.cloudevents.v1.proto.CloudEvent.parseFrom(protoBytes);
```

## 4.2 Parsing a Received CloudEvent

```java
// From the gRPC StreamObserver<CloudEvent>.onNext(value):
String eventType = value.getType();
String jsonPayload = value.getTextData();

// Deserialize based on type
switch (eventType) {
    case "CalculationMemberGreetEvent":
        GreetEvent greet = objectMapper.readValue(jsonPayload, GreetEvent.class);
        break;
    case "EntityProcessorCalculationRequest":
        ProcessorRequest req = objectMapper.readValue(jsonPayload, ProcessorRequest.class);
        break;
    // ... etc
}
```

# 5. Connection Lifecycle

## 5.1 Open the Stream

```java
StreamObserver<CloudEvent> requestObserver = asyncStub.startStreaming(
    new StreamObserver<CloudEvent>() {
        @Override
        public void onNext(CloudEvent value) {
            // Dispatch based on value.getType() — see Sections 6–8
        }

        @Override
        public void onError(Throwable t) {
            // Stream ended with a gRPC status — act on it per Section 12.1
        }

        @Override
        public void onCompleted() {
            // Server closed the stream — trigger reconnect
        }
    }
);
```

## 5.2 Join Handshake

Immediately after opening the stream, send a `CalculationMemberJoinEvent`:

```json
{
  "id": "<uuid>",
  "tags": ["approval-service", "notification"],
  "joinedLegalEntityId": "acme"
}
```

- **`tags`** route callouts to the member. See [tag matching](#521-tag-matching) below.
- **`joinedLegalEntityId`** is optional and holds your tenant id. The member always joins the tenant of its bearer token. When the field is present and not empty it must equal that tenant exactly, or the stream ends with `PermissionDenied` and nothing is registered. Sending it makes a misconfigured tenant fail at join time instead of leaving the member waiting for callouts that never come.

The server responds with a `CalculationMemberGreetEvent`, always the first event on the stream:

```json
{
  "id": "b914c3f1-3cdc-401b-89db-a1262d513465",
  "memberId": "b914c3f1-3cdc-401b-89db-a1262d513465",
  "joinedLegalEntityId": "acme",
  "success": true
}
```

`memberId` is the server-assigned member id; `joinedLegalEntityId` is the tenant the member joined. A join that fails does not produce a greet: the stream ends with a gRPC status (`InvalidArgument` for a malformed join, `PermissionDenied` for the wrong kind of token or a tenant mismatch). See [Section 14](#14-troubleshooting).

### 5.2.1 Tag matching

A processor, function criterion or schedule function names the members it may go to in `config.calculationNodesTags`, a comma-separated list. A member matches when it declares **at least one** of those tags: the sets need only overlap. Tags are compared exactly, letter case included; surrounding whitespace in the list is ignored. When `calculationNodesTags` is empty, every member of the tenant matches.

Among the matching members of the tenant, the server picks **round robin**: the member picked longest ago goes next, and a member that has just joined goes first. A member of another tenant is never chosen. To make sure one particular member receives a callout, give it a tag of its own.

### 5.3 Keep-Alive

The server sends each member a `CalculationMemberKeepAliveEvent` every `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL` seconds (default `10`):

```json
{
  "id": "b914c3f1-3cdc-401b-89db-a1262d513465",
  "memberId": "b914c3f1-3cdc-401b-89db-a1262d513465",
  "success": true
}
```

Answer each probe with an `EventAckResponse` whose `sourceEventId` is the probe's `id`:

```json
{
  "id": "<new-uuid>",
  "sourceEventId": "<id of the probe>",
  "success": true
}
```

You may also send keep-alives of your own. The server does not reply to a keep-alive or an ack that a member sends: it records the activity and nothing more. If your handler waits for a reply after it sends a keep-alive, remove that wait.

Anything the member sends counts as activity: an ack, a keep-alive, or a processor, criteria or function response. The server evicts a member, and ends its stream with `DeadlineExceeded`, when either of two things lasts `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT` seconds (default `30`):

- it has seen nothing from the member;
- one server-to-client write to the member has stalled. This catches a member that keeps sending keep-alives while its application has stopped reading the stream.

Every callout in flight on an evicted member fails with `COMPUTE_MEMBER_DISCONNECTED`.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL` | `10` s | Interval between server keep-alive probes; also the HTTP/2 transport keepalive idle time. |
| `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT` | `30` s | Silence or write stall after which the server **evicts the member and ends the stream**; also the transport keepalive ack timeout. |

<Aside type="caution" title="Going idle costs you the stream">

There is no intermediate "marked not alive but still registered" state that a
later probe recovers from. Exceeding `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT` ends the stream.
Read the stream continuously, keep your keep-alive handling fast and
non-blocking, and implement the reconnection logic in
[Section 12.1](#121-reconnection-strategy).

</Aside>

A slow consumer applies back pressure to its own stream only, not to the
streams of other members.

# 6. Handling Processor Requests

When an entity's workflow reaches a processor whose `calculationNodesTags` match your member's tags, the platform sends an `EntityProcessorCalculationRequest`.

## 6.1 Request Schema

```json
{
  "id": "f71b5020-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16",
  "requestId": "f71b5020-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16",
  "entityId": "f71b4ba2-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16",
  "processorId": "enrich-invoice",
  "processorName": "enrich-invoice",
  "workflow": { "id": "invoice-wf", "name": "invoice-wf" },
  "transition": { "id": "submit", "name": "submit" },
  "transactionId": "f71b4b8e-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16",
  "parameters": "{\"key\": \"value\"}",
  "success": true,
  "payload": {
    "type": "JSON",
    "data": { "invoiceId": "I-1", "amount": 10 },
    "meta": {
      "id": "f71b4ba2-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16",
      "modelKey": { "name": "invoice", "version": 1 },
      "state": "NEW",
      "creationDate": "2024-01-03T10:00:51.048963Z",
      "lastUpdateTime": "2024-01-03T10:00:51.048963Z",
      "transactionId": "f71b4b8e-e6c0-11f1-a29a-ae468cd3ed16"
    }
  }
}
```

**Key fields**:
- `requestId`: echo it back in the response. Every try of one callout carries the same `requestId`; see [Section 12.4](#124-idempotency).
- `entityId`: the entity being processed. Echo it back.
- `processorName`: route to your handler on this.
- `parameters`: the processor's `config.context` string, forwarded verbatim as a JSON **string**, not parsed. Absent when `context` is empty.
- `payload`: the entity, present unless the processor sets `attachEntity: false`. `payload.meta.transactionId` is the transaction making this version of the entity.

The CloudEvent envelope also carries attributes outside `text_data`: the identity attributes (see [Section 9](#9-auth-context-on-incoming-requests)), the transaction token `cyodatxtoken` (see [Section 10.3.1](#1031-transaction-joined-callbacks)), and the platform time in `time`. A compute node that computes an absolute time reads it from `time`, not from its own clock, so that the result agrees with the platform clock when that clock has been set (see [Controlling time](/build/testing-with-digital-twins/#controlling-time)).

## 6.2 Response Schema

```json
{
  "id": "<new-uuid>",
  "requestId": "<echo-request-id>",
  "entityId": "<echo-entity-id>",
  "success": true,
  "payload": {
    "type": "JSON",
    "data": { "invoiceId": "I-1", "amount": 10, "riskScore": 3 }
  },
  "warnings": []
}
```

**How the server reads an answer.** Answers are decoded strictly and follow these rules:

1. **`id`, `requestId` and `entityId`** identify the answer. `id` is the response event's own new id; `requestId` and `entityId` are copied from the request.
2. **`success` is optional and defaults to `true`.** An answer that leaves it out has reported success. The smallest successful answer is `{"id": "...", "requestId": "...", "entityId": "..."}`: the processor ran, changed nothing, and the workflow carries on.
3. **Only `success: false` reports a failure.** An `error` object on its own does not: an answer with an `error` and no `success: false` is a success, and its message reaches nobody. Send `error` only together with `success: false`, and never as `"error": null`.
4. **An answer the server cannot read fails the callout at once** with `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED`, not retryable, and no other member is tried. Unreadable means: `"success": null`, a member name in the wrong letter case (`"Success"`) or not declared by the schema, a duplicate member, a field of the wrong type, a `payload` that is not an object, or an `error` or `reason` containing the character U+0000. Nothing in such an answer is read, its `warnings` included; the client's error message says what was wrong.
5. **`payload.data`** replaces the entity's data when it is not null. When `payload` is absent, or `payload.data` is null, the entity is left as it is and the transition continues.
6. **Returned data is checked like a client write.** It must satisfy the model's schema, and a field the model does not declare is accepted only where the model's `changeLevel` would accept it from a client. Otherwise the transition fails with `WORKFLOW_FAILED` and rolls back.

A processor changes its own entity **only** through the data it returns. It never writes or deletes that entity through the API, with or without the transaction token; see [Section 10.3.1](#1031-transaction-joined-callbacks).

## 6.3 Error Response

```json
{
  "id": "<new-uuid>",
  "requestId": "<echo-request-id>",
  "entityId": "<echo-entity-id>",
  "success": false,
  "error": {
    "code": "BUSINESS_ERROR",
    "message": "credit check failed",
    "retryable": true
  }
}
```

A `success: false` answer is the callout's outcome. **No other member is tried**, whatever the processor's `retryPolicy`. The client's operation fails with `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED`; the detail carries your `error.message` (cut to 512 characters), and the response carries `retryable: true` exactly when your `error.retryable` was `true`:

```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "WORKFLOW_FAILED: processor enrich-invoice failed: credit check failed",
  "instance": "/entity/JSON/invoice/1",
  "properties": { "errorCode": "WORKFLOW_FAILED", "retryable": true }
}
```

`retryable` tells the *client* that running the whole operation again may succeed. It does not make the server try another member. The exception is an `ASYNC_NEW_TX` processor: its failure is logged, its savepoint is undone, and the operation continues.

### 6.3.1 Errors the client of the operation sees

Separately from errors *you* return, the platform reports failures to deliver or complete a callout. These apply to all three callout kinds:

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NO_COMPUTE_MEMBER_FOR_TAG` | `503`, retryable | No matching member appeared, on any node, within `CYODA_DISPATCH_WAIT_TIMEOUT` (default `5s`). No try was made. |
| `COMPUTE_MEMBER_DISCONNECTED` | `503`, retryable | The member's stream dropped after it was given the work (single try). |
| `DISPATCH_TIMEOUT` | `503`, retryable | No answer within `responseTimeoutMs` (single try). |
| `DISPATCH_FORWARD_FAILED` | `503`, retryable | The answer of the cluster node the callout was handed to was lost (single try). |
| `CALLOUT_FAILED` | `503`, retryable | More than one try failed; the message lists them. |
| `WORKFLOW_FAILED` | `400` | The member answered `success: false` (retryable when the member said so), or its answer could not be read (not retryable). |
| `TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK_ONLY` | `409`, not retryable | A callback's write failed with an error that is not retryable, which made the transaction rollback-only. The message names the code the callback got. |
| `CONFLICT` | `409`, retryable | A callback's write had already lost a race against another transaction. This takes precedence over the member's answer. |

See [Section 10.5](#105-retry-policies) for when a callout is tried on another member.

---

# 7. Handling Criteria Requests

A criterion with a `function` condition is evaluated by a compute node. The platform sends one `EntityCriteriaCalculationRequest` for each function condition that the criterion's evaluation reaches. A function condition inside a group that short-circuits before it, or one whose pre-check did not match, is not called. The grouping rules are in [Workflows and processors](/build/workflows-and-processors/).

## 7.1 Request Schema

```json
{
  "id": "3e93c162-e6c1-11f1-8830-ae468cd3ed16",
  "requestId": "3e93c162-e6c1-11f1-8830-ae468cd3ed16",
  "entityId": "3e93bef6-e6c1-11f1-8830-ae468cd3ed16",
  "criteriaId": "is-low-risk",
  "criteriaName": "is-low-risk",
  "target": "TRANSITION",
  "workflow": { "id": "claim-wf", "name": "claim-wf" },
  "transition": { "id": "auto-approve", "name": "auto-approve" },
  "transactionId": "3e93bed8-e6c1-11f1-8830-ae468cd3ed16",
  "success": true,
  "payload": {
    "type": "JSON",
    "data": { "claimId": "C-2" },
    "meta": { "...": "same shape as a processor request" }
  }
}
```

**The `target` field** says where the criterion sits:

| Target | Meaning | Available Context |
|---|---|---|
| `WORKFLOW` | Workflow-selection criterion (does this workflow apply?) | `workflow` |
| `TRANSITION` | Transition criterion (should this transition fire?) | `workflow`, `transition` |

The published schema also lists `PROCESSOR` and `NA`. cyoda-go does not send them.

The envelope carries the same identity, `cyodatxtoken` and `time` attributes as a processor request.

## 7.2 Response Schema

```json
{
  "id": "<new-uuid>",
  "requestId": "<echo-request-id>",
  "entityId": "<echo-entity-id>",
  "success": true,
  "matches": false,
  "reason": "order total 4200 exceeds the 1000 auto-approval limit"
}
```

**Key fields**:
- `requestId`, `entityId`: copied from the request, as for a processor.
- `matches`: **required** on every answer except an explicit `success: false`. `true` means the criterion is satisfied. An answer that omits `matches` is not read as `false`: it is an unreadable answer and fails the operation with `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED`. The `success` default fills in the flag, never the verdict.
- `reason`: optional explanation for a `false` result; see below.

The answer rules of [Section 6.2](#62-response-schema) apply here as well. A criteria answer with `success: false` does **not** evaluate to `false`: it fails the operation with `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED` (`failed to evaluate transition criterion: <message>`), `retryable` when your error said so.

Criteria must have no side effects, inside cyoda or outside it. The platform treats them as safe to repeat and gives them to another member whenever one does not answer.

### 7.2.1 Explaining a `false` result

`reason` reaches the caller and the audit trail, so populate it on every
`false`. It is kept to its first 2048 characters, marked with `…` when cut.

Where it surfaces depends on how the criterion was reached:

- **A transition the client named**, rejected by its criterion, appends the
  reason to the `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED` detail:
  `transition "<name>" criterion not matched: <reason>`. This is the
  guaranteed, backend-independent surface.
- **Automated cascade and workflow-selection paths** record it durably on the
  state-machine audit trail: `TRANSITION_NOT_MATCH_CRITERION` carries it in
  `data.reason`, and so does `WORKFLOW_SKIP`.

If you omit a reason, the audit trail falls back to `"criterion did not match"`
and the `400` detail is left bare (`criterion not matched`), so the caller learns
nothing. Write the specific cause: `"order total 4200 exceeds the 1000
auto-approval limit"` beats `"validation failed"`. When a function condition
sits in a group, the reason lists every function condition the evaluation
reached and what each answered.

---

# 8. Handling Function Requests

A **Function** callout is the third request shape your compute node may
receive, alongside Processor and Criteria. The three differ in what they are
allowed to do:

| Callout | Returns | Mutates the entity? |
|---|---|---|
| Processor | an updated entity payload | Yes, through the returned data only |
| Criteria | a boolean `matches` | No |
| **Function** | a **declared typed value** | No |

A Function computes and returns a value without side effects. The response
carries a `resultKind` discriminator naming the shape of `result`, so the
caller can validate what it receives.

## 8.1 Request Schema

The request is an `EntityFunctionCalculationRequest`. It mirrors a processor
request, but the callout target is named by **`functionId` / `functionName`**;
there is no `processorName` on this message, so route on `functionName`.

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `requestId` | YES | Echo back unchanged. |
| `entityId` | YES | Echo back unchanged. |
| `functionId` | YES | Identifier of the invoked function. |
| `functionName` | YES | **The routing key**: the registered `schedule.function.name`. Dispatch on this. |
| `workflow` | YES | The workflow this callout belongs to. |
| `transition` | NO | The transition carrying the schedule. |
| `transactionId` | NO | The originating transaction. |
| `payload` | NO | The entity data, present unless `attachEntity` is `false`. |
| `parameters` | NO | The configured `context` string, forwarded verbatim. |

## 8.2 Response Schema

```json
{
  "id": "<new-uuid>",
  "requestId": "<echo-request-id>",
  "entityId": "<echo-entity-id>",
  "success": true,
  "resultKind": "Schedule",
  "result": { "fireAfterMs": 3600000, "expireAfterMs": 600000 }
}
```

- `resultKind` names the shape of `result`. **`"Schedule"` is currently the
  only defined kind.**
- `result` is the typed value itself.
- The answer rules of [Section 6.2](#62-response-schema) apply: `success`
  defaults to `true`, and only `success: false` reports a failure, which fails
  the callout as it does for a processor (no other member is tried; the message
  and `retryable` reach the client).

## 8.3 The `Schedule` result kind

`Schedule` drives a
[scheduled transition's](/build/scheduled-transitions/)
`schedule.function`, computing when a transition should fire for one specific
entity:

- **Fire time** (required): exactly one of `fireAt` (absolute epoch-ms) or
  `fireAfterMs` (relative to arm time).
- **Expiry** (optional): at most one of `expireAt` or `expireAfterMs`, the
  latter relative to the *resolved fire time* rather than to arm time.

Compute an absolute `fireAt` from the request's CloudEvent `time` attribute,
the platform clock, not from your own clock.

<Aside type="caution" title="This callout runs inside the caller's write transaction">

It is invoked synchronously while the entity write that arms the timer is
still open, and it is invoked again on *every* re-arm, not once per entity.
Like every callout it may also be tried on another member, so the same
request can run twice. A slow handler slows every write to that entity; a
failing or unreachable handler **fails the write**. Keep it fast,
side-effect free, and dependent only on data you already have.

Returning a malformed `result`, or one that does not match the declared
`resultKind`, fails the write with `500 SCHEDULE_FUNCTION_INVALID_RESULT`.

</Aside>

---

# 9. Auth Context on Incoming Requests

Every processor, criteria and function request carries identity attributes. They name two principals:

- the **attributed** principal: who the work is *for*;
- the **executor**: who *does* it.

The two differ whenever one party acts for another. A backend's on-behalf-of request is attributed to the user and executed by the backend's client. A scheduled transition is attributed to whoever armed it and executed by `system`.

## 9.1 Extension Attributes

The attributes are entries of the Protobuf CloudEvent's `attributes` map, each holding a string (`ce_string`). They are **not** inside the JSON `text_data` payload. An absent attribute has no entry.

| Attribute | Description |
|---|---|
| `authtype` | Kind of the attributed principal: `user`, `service` or `system`. |
| `authid` | Id of the attributed principal. |
| `authexectype` | Kind of the executor: `user`, `service` or `system`. |
| `authexecid` | Id of the executor. |
| `authclaims` | The **executor's** roles, comma separated. Never the user's: for an on-behalf-of request they are the on-behalf-of client's roles. Absent when the executor has no roles (the `system` executor of a scheduled fire). Never contains credentials. |

`authtype`, `authid` and `authclaims` are attributes of the [CloudEvents Auth Context extension](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec/blob/main/cloudevents/extensions/authcontext.md). `authexectype` and `authexecid` are cyoda's own.

A callout made in mock IAM mode, where the one mock principal is both, carries:

```
authtype=service      authid=mock-user-001
authexectype=service  authexecid=mock-user-001
authclaims=ROLE_ADMIN,ROLE_M2M
```

## 9.2 Auth Type Values

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user` | A person: the user an on-behalf-of token asserts, or the platform operator's `cyoda token`. |
| `service` | An M2M client acting as itself. |
| `system` | The platform itself, as the executor of a scheduled fire. |

The kinds are the principals' explicit kinds, recorded when each principal is established, never inferred from roles. The extension's own list uses `service_account` for a service; cyoda sends `service`.

If either principal has no id, or a kind that is unset or unrecognized, the platform **fails the callout dispatch** rather than sending a placeholder. A bogus or absent principal never reaches your compute node.

<Aside type="caution" title="The only values are user, service and system">

There is no `service_account`, `unauthenticated` or `unknown`. A handler that
switches on one of those strings never matches it. Do not rely on a `default`
or `else` branch to catch an unroutable principal either: the platform fails
the dispatch rather than sending one.

</Aside>

### Who is attributed, who executes

| Path | Attributed (`authtype` / `authid`) | Executor (`authexectype` / `authexecid`) |
|---|---|---|
| An on-behalf-of request for a user, and every callout of its cascade | the user (`user`) | the on-behalf-of client (`service`) |
| A client's own request, and its cascade | the client (`service`) | the same client |
| A compute node's callback that presents the transaction token (a write-back joined to the transaction), and its cascade | the transaction's origin: the user, client or arming principal that began it | the compute node's client (`service`) |
| A compute node's independent request, without the transaction token (for example the callback of a `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor with `startNewTxOnDispatch: false`), and its cascade | the compute node's client (`service`) | the same client |
| A scheduled fire, and every callout of its cascade | the principal that armed the timer | `system` (`system`) |
| A request with a `cyoda token` (the platform operator's) | the token's user (`user`) | the same (`user`), with the token's roles in `authclaims` |
| A callout handed over to another cluster node | as computed by the dispatching node | as computed by the dispatching node |

A `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor with `startNewTxOnDispatch: true` begins its new transaction with the origin of the one it committed, so its callout carries the principals of the request that reached it. Inside a scheduled fire, even a `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor dispatched outside a transaction carries the arming principal and the `system` executor.

**`authtype == "user"` does not mean "the user acted now".** It is also the value for a compute node's write-back inside that user's transaction, and for a scheduled fire the user armed. A check such as "the submitter may not approve" needs the executor too: require `authtype == "user"`, `authexectype == "service"` and `authexecid` on an allow-list of your backend's on-behalf-of client ids. The full recipe is in [`cyoda help auth integration`](/help/auth/integration/) (*Reading identity in a compute node*).

**There are no user roles in a callout.** cyoda carries none by design: your application decides what a user may do. When a processor needs that, look the user up by `authid` in your own directory, or have the backend record the facts the workflow needs in the entity's data before it calls cyoda.

**Trust the attributes only over TLS.** A compute node relies on them only if it verified the server certificate of the endpoint it connected to (see [Section 3](#3-connection-setup)).

## 9.3 Extracting Auth Context (Java/Kotlin)

The keys in the Protobuf CloudEvent's `attributes` map are the attribute names listed above, with no prefix:

```java
// From the gRPC StreamObserver<CloudEvent>.onNext(value):
Map<String, CloudEventAttributeValue> attrs = value.getAttributesMap();
String attributedType = attrs.get("authtype").getCeString();
String attributedId   = attrs.get("authid").getCeString();
String executorType   = attrs.get("authexectype").getCeString();
String executorId     = attrs.get("authexecid").getCeString();
String claims = attrs.containsKey("authclaims")
    ? attrs.get("authclaims").getCeString()
    : null;

// Roles are a comma-separated string, NOT JSON.
List<String> executorRoles = (claims == null || claims.isEmpty())
    ? List.of()
    : Arrays.asList(claims.split(","));
```

The exact accessor depends on your gRPC tooling. In Python, use dict-like indexing on `.attributes`; in Go, the generated message's `GetAttributes()` method.

**Go compute nodes** can use the public package
`github.com/cyoda/cyoda-go/api/grpc/authctx`. Every function takes a
`*cloudevents.CloudEvent` from `github.com/cyoda/cyoda-go/api/grpc/cloudevents`:

- `Type(ce)` and `ID(ce)` return the attributed principal;
- `ExecutorType(ce)` and `ExecutorID(ce)` return the executor (`""` when absent);
- `Roles(ce)` returns the executor's roles (`nil` when absent);
- `Require(ce, role)` is a **fail-closed** role gate: it returns `true` only
  when the executor is a `service` and `role` is in `authclaims`. The
  attributed principal plays no part in it, so a scheduled fire (executor
  `system`) never passes.

The package works only on that module's generated CloudEvent type. A compute
node with its own generated types reads the `attributes` map directly: the
attribute names and values are the contract, not the package.

## 9.4 Example Claims

`authclaims` is a flat comma-separated list of the executor's role names. For a
plain client, or for the on-behalf-of client of a user's request:

```
ROLE_M2M
```

For a request made with an operator's `cyoda token` signed with two roles:

```
ROLE_ADMIN,ROLE_M2M
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Do not parse authclaims as JSON">

`objectMapper.readValue(authClaims, Map.class)` throws on
`ROLE_ADMIN,ROLE_M2M`. Split on `,`. Go clients should use `authctx.Roles`,
which does exactly this.

</Aside>

## 9.5 Use Cases

- **Audit logging**: record which user the work was for (`authid`) and which part of the system did it (`authexecid`).
- **Segregation of duties**: refuse an approval whose attributed user submitted the item, as described above.
- **Business decisions**: branch on whether the work is a user's request, a client's own work, or a scheduled fire.
- **Debugging**: trace a processing failure back to the originating request.

Callouts never cross tenants: a member receives only callouts of the tenant it joined.

---

# 10. Workflow Configuration

Your compute node does not exist in isolation: workflow configurations on the platform side invoke it. This section describes how workflows reference externalized processors and criteria, so that you understand the relationship between your member's tags and handlers and the platform configuration. The full workflow schema is in [Workflows and processors](/build/workflows-and-processors/).

## 10.1 Externalized Processor in Workflow JSON

```json
{
  "importMode": "REPLACE",
  "workflows": [{
    "version": "1.5",
    "name": "invoice-wf",
    "initialState": "NEW",
    "active": true,
    "states": {
      "NEW": {
        "transitions": [{
          "name": "submit",
          "next": "SUBMITTED",
          "manual": false,
          "processors": [{
            "type": "externalized",
            "name": "enrich-invoice",
            "executionMode": "SYNC",
            "config": {
              "attachEntity": true,
              "calculationNodesTags": "invoice-service",
              "responseTimeoutMs": 5000,
              "retryPolicy": "FIXED",
              "idempotent": true,
              "context": "{\"key\": \"value\"}"
            }
          }]
        }]
      },
      "SUBMITTED": {}
    }
  }]
}
```

Import it with `POST /api/model/{entityName}/{modelVersion}/workflow/import`.

## 10.2 Processor Configuration Fields

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | `externalized` | The only value accepted. Any other value is refused at import with `400 VALIDATION_FAILED`. |
| `name` | string | (required) | The processor name. Sent as `processorName` in the request. |
| `executionMode` | string | `SYNC` | One of `SYNC`, `ASYNC_SAME_TX`, `ASYNC_NEW_TX`, `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH`. Empty means `SYNC`. See [Section 10.3](#103-execution-modes). |
| `config.attachEntity` | boolean | `true` | Whether to send the entity in the request payload. Set it to `false` explicitly to opt out. |
| `config.calculationNodesTags` | string | `""` | Comma-separated tags. A member matches when it declares at least one of them; empty matches every member of the tenant. See [Section 5.2.1](#521-tag-matching). |
| `config.responseTimeoutMs` | integer | `CYODA_CALLOUT_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS` (`30000`) | How long one try waits for a member's answer. `0` or absent means the server default. A value above `CYODA_CALLOUT_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS` (default `60000`) is refused at import. |
| `config.retryPolicy` | string | `FIXED` | `NONE`: one try. `FIXED` or absent: one try plus `CYODA_RETRY_FIXED_NUM_RETRIES` (default `3`), so four tries. There is no delay between tries. See [Section 10.5](#105-retry-policies). |
| `config.idempotent` | boolean | `false` | Your declaration that the processor may run more than once for one callout, partly or at the same time on two members, with the same outcome as running it once, in cyoda and in every system it touches. Lets the platform give the work to another member after one went quiet. |
| `config.context` | string | (none) | Forwarded verbatim as the `parameters` string of the request. Use it to serve several workflow roles from one handler. |
| `startNewTxOnDispatch` | boolean | `false` | Sibling of `config`, not inside it. Valid only with `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH`; refused with any other mode. With `true`, a new transaction is opened before dispatch and the processor's callbacks join it. |

`config.asyncResult: true` and any `config.crossoverToAsyncMs` are refused at import with `400 VALIDATION_FAILED`: cyoda-go does not implement them.

## 10.3 Execution Modes

| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `SYNC` | The engine dispatches and blocks until the answer arrives; the entity's transaction stays open during the wait. A failed callout fails the operation and the entity stays in its source state. |
| `ASYNC_SAME_TX` | Same dispatch and failure behaviour as `SYNC`: it blocks inline, in the same transaction. |
| `ASYNC_NEW_TX` | Dispatched inside a **savepoint** of the same transaction. On a processor failure the savepoint is undone, a warning is logged, its returned data is discarded, and the operation continues to the next processor. |
| `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` | Commits the work so far before dispatching, releasing the storage connection during the external compute. The entity is then durable in its pre-callout state. The result is applied in a new transaction by compare-and-save; if another transaction changed the entity meanwhile, the operation fails with `412 ENTITY_MODIFIED`. The recommended mode for slow external work. |

`SYNC` is the simplest starting point. A `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor must be idempotent, or detect prior completion with a key of its own, because a client that repeats the operation dispatches it again with a new `requestId`. What each mode leaves behind on failure is set out in [Workflows and processors](/build/workflows-and-processors/#processors).

### 10.3.1 Transaction-joined callbacks

A processor, a function criterion or a schedule function may call back into the platform while it handles a callout: read entities, search, write other entities. Such a request is a **callback**.

Before each try of a callout, the engine mints a signed transaction token and attaches it to the request as the `cyodatxtoken` CloudEvent attribute. A callback that echoes it, as the `X-Tx-Token` HTTP header or the `tx-token` gRPC metadata, **joins the callout's transaction**. Every callback also carries the compute node's own current `client_credentials` token as its bearer. A callback without the transaction token is an independent request in a transaction of its own: the normal case for a `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor with `startNewTxOnDispatch: false`, whose callout carries no token.

**What a joined callback sees.** A read, search, count or page under the token sees the entity the callout runs for as the workflow has it at the moment of the callout, and sees what earlier callbacks of the same transaction wrote. These writes are uncommitted and provisional until the operation that owns the transaction commits. A read with `pointInTime` selects committed state, even inside a joined transaction; omit it to read what this transaction has written. An entity this transaction created, read with `pointInTime`, answers `404 ENTITY_NOT_FOUND`.

**The rules a compute node must follow:**

- **Never write the entity the callout runs for.** A processor changes its entity only through the data it returns. No callback writes or deletes that entity, with or without the token, and no callback writes any entity whose cascade is running in the same transaction. Such a write starts the entity's workflow again inside its own cascade, which can loop without end. Read the entity under the token, or from the request's payload.
- **Send the callbacks of one transaction in series.** On the in-tree backends (memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL) each callback holds the transaction while the server works on it, so callbacks sent in parallel are served one at a time. When a callback's write runs a workflow with a callout of its own, other callbacks of the transaction are refused with `503 TRANSACTION_BUSY` (retryable) until that inner callout is answered. At most `CYODA_CALLOUT_JOINED_MAX_WAITERS` (default `128`) callbacks may wait; past that, `503 TOO_MANY_JOINED_REQUESTS` (retryable, after a short back-off).
- **Each callback is all-or-nothing.** A `2xx` answer means all its writes were kept in the transaction; any error means none were. A schema extension a write made stays either way. After a retryable error, send the callback again under the same token. A **write** that fails with an error that is not retryable makes the transaction rollback-only: the callout is stopped, and the operation fails with `409 TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK_ONLY` (under an `ASYNC_NEW_TX` processor, that processor fails instead and the operation continues). A failed read marks nothing.
- **A token belongs to one try of one callout.** Once the server has given the callout to another member, or the callout has ended, a callback bearing the token is refused with `410 CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED` while the transaction is open, and `404 TRANSACTION_NOT_FOUND` once it has closed. A callback still running at that moment completes, is discarded, and is answered `410 CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED`. A token past its expiry is refused with `410 TRANSACTION_EXPIRED`; a malformed token with `401 UNAUTHORIZED`. None of these is retryable: stop working on that request.
- **A callback never commits the transaction it joined.** A callback write that reaches a `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor is refused with `409 COMMIT_IN_JOINED_TRANSACTION`, and makes the transaction rollback-only. Make such a write as an independent request, without the token.
- **A callback never administers a model or a workflow.** A request under the token that would import, delete, lock, unlock, change the level of, or set the unique keys of a model, or import a workflow, is refused with `400 MODEL_ADMIN_IN_JOINED_TRANSACTION` before anything is read or written.
- **A joined callback cannot carry its own deadline or batching.** `transactionTimeoutMillis`, `transactionSize`, `transactionWindow` and search's `timeoutMillis` are refused with `400` on a callback that joins a transaction. A collection write runs as one unit.
- **Keep answers small.** A callback's request body is limited to 10 MiB, and its answer to `CYODA_CALLOUT_JOINED_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES` (default 10 MiB): a larger answer fails with `413 JOINED_RESPONSE_TOO_LARGE`. Page large reads with `pageSize` and `pageNumber`.
- **An edge message is not part of the transaction.** A message a processor saves stays even when the transaction rolls back, and is saved again if the processor is repeated. Make the save idempotent and attach the message id to the entity that owns it.

Over gRPC, these errors arrive in the RPC's error envelope (`success: false`, `error.code` `CLIENT_ERROR`, `error.message` starting with the code), not as a gRPC status. A failing bearer token is the gRPC status `Unauthenticated`.

A callback is not abandoned when the member's connection drops, or when a deadline the member sets on its own call passes: once it has its turn on the transaction it runs to completion. If the connection drops, the outcome of a write is unknown; do not assume it failed.

**Server settings** (see the [configuration reference](/reference/configuration/#all-variables)):

- `CYODA_CALLOUT_PASS_ALLOWANCE` (default `30s`): how long the transaction token outlives its try's answer limit.
- `CYODA_CALLOUT_JOINED_MAX_WAITERS` (default `128`) and `CYODA_CALLOUT_JOINED_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES` (default 10 MiB): the limits above.
- `CYODA_GRPC_NODE_ADDR`: in a cluster, this node's gRPC endpoint advertised to peers, which forward callbacks to the node that holds the transaction.

The `CYODA_COMPUTE_*` variables in `cyoda help config grpc` are a convention of cyoda's own test compute node. The server does not read them, and your compute node may take its endpoint and credentials from any configuration.

## 10.4 Externalized Criteria (`type: function`) in Workflow JSON

```json
{
  "name": "auto-approve",
  "next": "APPROVED",
  "manual": false,
  "criterion": {
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
      "name": "is-low-risk",
      "config": {
        "attachEntity": true,
        "calculationNodesTags": "invoice-service",
        "responseTimeoutMs": 5000,
        "retryPolicy": "NONE"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Function criteria use the same `config` fields as processors, apart from `idempotent`, which a criterion's `config` refuses with `400 VALIDATION_FAILED`: a criterion is treated as repeat-safe by rule.

## 10.5 Retry Policies

A **try** is one attempt to hand a callout to one compute member. Every try of one callout carries the same `requestId`, the same `id` and the same `transactionId`. Tries follow one after another with no delay.

| Policy | Tries |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | One try. |
| `FIXED` (or absent) | One try plus `CYODA_RETRY_FIXED_NUM_RETRIES` (default `3`), so four tries. The number is set on the server, not in the workflow. |

Whether another member is tried depends on how far the work got:

- **The work never reached a member** (it had gone, or was not taking data): another member is tried, for every callout kind.
- **The work reached the member, then no answer within `responseTimeoutMs`, or its connection dropped**: another member is tried for a criterion, a function, or a processor with `idempotent: true`. For any other processor **nothing else is tried**, and the callout fails. This is the repeat rule: a member that went quiet may still have done the work, inside cyoda or outside it.
- **The member answered `success: false`, or its answer could not be read**: nothing else is tried, whatever `idempotent` says.

**Waiting for a member is not a try.** When no matching member is attached anywhere, the callout waits up to `CYODA_DISPATCH_WAIT_TIMEOUT` (default `5s`, once per callout) and continues the moment one attaches, then fails with `503 NO_COMPUTE_MEMBER_FOR_TAG`. This applies with `retryPolicy: NONE` too.

**Time is the hard limit.** In a cluster a callout can be handed to peer nodes with the tries that are left, so the number of tries is the normal number rather than a hard limit. A callout never runs longer than `tries × answer limit + CYODA_DISPATCH_WAIT_TIMEOUT + CYODA_CALLOUT_HANDOVER_ALLOWANCE`, which is 155 s at the defaults.

---

# 11. BaseEvent Schema

All events on the stream extend the `BaseEvent` schema:

```json
{
  "id": "<string, required>",
  "success": true,
  "error": {
    "code": "<string, required if error>",
    "message": "<string, required if error>",
    "retryable": false
  },
  "warnings": ["<optional array of warning strings>"]
}
```

- `id`: every event must have a unique ID (UUID recommended).
- `success`: optional; defaults to `true`. Send `false` explicitly to report a failure. `null` is not a valid value.
- `error`: send it only with `success: false`; never send `"error": null`. `code` and `message` are required within it.
- `warnings`: optional array of warning strings. The warnings of an answer that was read reach the client.

---

# 12. Production Robustness

## 12.1 Reconnection Strategy

gRPC streams end for network problems, server restarts and rolling upgrades, client changes, and evictions. Act on the status the stream ended with:

| Status | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Unauthenticated` | Missing or invalid token; or the client was deleted, or its secret reset, since the token was issued | Read the current credentials, fetch a new token, reconnect. If a freshly fetched token is refused again, the client is gone: stop and alert, do not loop. |
| `Unavailable` | The node is shutting down (it closes open streams within 10 seconds of `SIGTERM`), a send failed, or the client store could not be read | Reconnect with backoff, through the load balancer, to any node. |
| `Internal` | The server failed to build a message | Reconnect with backoff; report it if it repeats. |
| `DeadlineExceeded` | Evicted for silence or a stalled write | Reconnect at once, and fix the cause: read the stream continuously and answer keep-alives. |
| `PermissionDenied` | Wrong kind of token, or `joinedLegalEntityId` names another tenant | Fix the configuration. Do not reconnect in a loop. |
| `InvalidArgument` | The first message was not a valid join, or a CloudEvent was malformed | Fix the client. Do not reconnect in a loop. |

For the statuses you reconnect on:

1. **Back off exponentially**: start at 1 second, cap at 60 seconds.
2. **Re-join after reconnect**: every new stream requires a fresh `CalculationMemberJoinEvent`.
3. **Use a current token**: fetch a new one before reconnecting if the cached one is near expiry.

```
┌──────────┐    onError/onCompleted    ┌──────────┐    delay    ┌──────────────┐    success    ┌──────┐
│ Connected│ ────────────────────────► │ Backoff  │ ────────► │ Reconnecting │ ────────────► │ Join │
└──────────┘                           └──────────┘           └──────────────┘              └──────┘
     ▲                                                              │ failure                   │
     │                                                              ▼                           │
     │                                                        ┌──────────┐                      │
     │                                                        │ Backoff  │ (increase delay)      │
     │                                                        └──────────┘                      │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                              Greet received
```

## 12.2 Thread Safety

The gRPC `StreamObserver` is **not thread-safe**, and gRPC forbids concurrent sends on one stream. If your business logic runs on multiple threads, synchronize all calls to `observer.onNext()`:

```java
synchronized (requestObserver) {
    requestObserver.onNext(cloudEvent);
}
```

## 12.3 Response Timeouts

Each try waits for your answer for the callout's `responseTimeoutMs`, or the server's `CYODA_CALLOUT_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS` (default **30 seconds**) when the callout sets none. When a try times out:

- the try has failed;
- another member is tried only under the rules of [Section 10.5](#105-retry-policies): for a processor, only if it is `idempotent`;
- an answer that arrives late is discarded, and callbacks under that try's transaction token are refused with `410 CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED`.

Design your business logic to complete well within the timeout, accounting for network latency.

## 12.4 Idempotency

The same callout can reach your compute node more than once: on another member after a timeout or a dropped connection, or on the same member after it reconnects. Every try of one callout carries the same `requestId`, so a member, or a de-duplication store shared by several members, can recognise a repeat by it.

`requestId` does **not** cover a new callout that does the same work: the client repeating the operation, the scheduler retrying a scheduled run, or a `COMMIT_BEFORE_DISPATCH` processor dispatched again. Each is a new callout with a new `requestId`. Recognise those by a key of your own.

What is safe to repeat:

- **Inside cyoda.** A member that has been replaced is shut out: its callbacks are refused with `CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED`. "Set this field to X" is safe to repeat; "add 10 to the balance" is not. "Create an entity" is never safe to repeat as it stands: check first whether the entity already exists.
- **Outside cyoda.** Charging a card, sending a message or calling another service is not part of a cyoda transaction. A rollback does not undo it, and a repeat does it again. Use `requestId` as the idempotency key the other system sees, or compensate.
- **Criteria and functions** must have no side effects at all. The platform repeats them freely.
- **A processor that only returns changed data**, with no callbacks and no outside effects, is trivially safe: mark it `idempotent: true`.

## 12.5 Graceful Shutdown

When shutting down your client:

1. Stop accepting new requests (drain in-flight work).
2. Complete any pending responses and send them.
3. Close the gRPC stream via `requestObserver.onCompleted()`.
4. Shut down the `ManagedChannel` with a grace period:
   ```java
   channel.shutdown().awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
   ```

The platform sees the stream close. Callouts in flight on the member fail with `COMPUTE_MEMBER_DISCONNECTED` and are tried on another member where [Section 10.5](#105-retry-policies) allows.

## 12.6 Multiple Members

Run **several members** with the same tags, in one process or several, for horizontal scaling and high availability. The platform spreads callouts over the matching members of the tenant round robin, and in a cluster a node tries its own members before handing a callout to a peer. Running at least two members keeps processing going while one is down. All replicas of one compute-node service share its client.

## 12.7 Monitoring

Track these metrics in your client:
- **Request count** by type (processor, criteria, function) and result (success, failure)
- **Response latency** (time from receiving a request to sending its answer)
- **Repeated `requestId`s** (callouts that reached you more than once)
- **Reconnection count and frequency**, by gRPC status
- **Callback errors** by code (`CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED`, `TRANSACTION_BUSY`, `TOO_MANY_JOINED_REQUESTS`)

# 13. Quick Reference — Message Flow

```
Client                                          Server
  │                                                │
  │──── startStreaming() ─────────────────────────►│   (open stream with the client's own token)
  │                                                │
  │──── CalculationMemberJoinEvent ───────────────►│   (register with tags)
  │◄─── CalculationMemberGreetEvent ───────────────│   (server confirms, assigns memberId)
  │                                                │
  │◄─── CalculationMemberKeepAliveEvent ───────────│   (periodic liveness probe)
  │──── EventAckResponse ─────────────────────────►│   (ack the probe)
  │                                                │
  │◄─── EntityProcessorCalculationRequest ─────────│   (process this entity)
  │       ┄┄ callbacks over HTTP/gRPC, in series,  │
  │          with tx-token + client token ┄┄       │
  │──── EntityProcessorCalculationResponse ───────►│   (here's the result)
  │                                                │
  │◄─── EntityCriteriaCalculationRequest ──────────│   (evaluate this criterion)
  │──── EntityCriteriaCalculationResponse ────────►│   (matches: true/false)
  │                                                │
  │──── CalculationMemberKeepAliveEvent ──────────►│   (optional; the server does not reply)
  │                                                │
```

# 14. Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Unauthenticated` on stream open | Missing or invalid token | Send the client's current `client_credentials` token as `authorization: Bearer <token>`. |
| `Unauthenticated` on an open stream, or on reconnect with the old token | The client was deleted, or its secret was reset | Read the new secret from your secret store, fetch a new token, reconnect. If a fresh token is refused, stop and alert. |
| `PermissionDenied` on stream open | An on-behalf-of token, a `cyoda token`, or a token without `ROLE_M2M`; in mock mode, `CYODA_IAM_MOCK_KIND` is `user` or `system` | Use the compute node's own `client_credentials` token; in mock mode use the default `service` kind. |
| `PermissionDenied` after the join | `joinedLegalEntityId` is not the token's tenant | Set it to your tenant id, or leave it out. |
| Connection refused from another host or a container | The gRPC listener binds loopback by default | Set `CYODA_GRPC_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` on the server. |
| Stream closed with `DeadlineExceeded` | Nothing received within `CYODA_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT` (default 30 s), or a write to the member stalled | Read the stream continuously; keep the keep-alive handler fast and non-blocking. Reconnect per [Section 12.1](#121-reconnection-strategy). |
| Requests not arriving; client sees `503 NO_COMPUTE_MEMBER_FOR_TAG` | No tag in common with the callout's `calculationNodesTags`, or a letter-case difference, or the member joined another tenant | Declare at least one of the callout's tags, spelled exactly. Check the tenant in the greet. |
| Client sees `503 DISPATCH_TIMEOUT` or `CALLOUT_FAILED` | Business logic too slow | Make the handler faster, or raise `responseTimeoutMs` (up to `CYODA_CALLOUT_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MAX_MS`). |
| Client sees `400 WORKFLOW_FAILED` "could not be read" | The answer broke a rule of [Section 6.2](#62-response-schema): `"success": null`, a wrong-case or undeclared member, a missing `matches` | Send the members the schema declares, spelled exactly. |
| A failure is reported as a success | The answer carries `error` but not `success: false` | Send `success: false` with the `error`. |
| Same `requestId` received twice | The callout was given to this member again after a timeout or reconnect | Expected. De-duplicate on `requestId`. |
| Callback answered `410 CALLOUT_SUPERSEDED` | The try timed out and the callout moved on, or the callout ended | Stop working on that request; its writes are discarded. |
| Callback answered `503 TRANSACTION_BUSY` | Another callback of the transaction is paused in a callout of its own | Send callbacks in series; retry this one once the other has been answered. |
| Client sees `409 TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK_ONLY` | A callback write failed with an error that is not retryable | Look at the code named in the message and fix that callback. |
| `authtype` is `user` although no user acted now | The callout is part of a write-back inside the user's transaction, or a scheduled fire the user armed | Check `authexectype` and `authexecid` as well. See [Section 9.2](#92-auth-type-values). |
| `authexectype` is `system` | The callout is part of a scheduled fire | Expected. `authid` is the principal that armed the timer. |
| `authclaims` is missing | The executor has no roles: the `system` executor of a scheduled fire | Check `authexectype` before reading claims. |
| `authtype` is `service`, not `service_account` | `service_account` is not a value the platform emits | Switch on `service`. |
| Callout never arrives; dispatch fails | A principal's kind is unset or unrecognized | Dispatch fails closed rather than sending a bogus identity. Check how the originating request authenticated. |
